task_components.component_text: Identify and describe the kinetic sampling strategies (i.e., timing and frequency of sample collection) used in PFAS adsorption, removal, or degradation experiments, with attention to how early-time sampling is implemented to capture rapid initial uptake or fast reaction phases, when such behavior is reported.

Explain how later-time or endpoint sampling is scheduled in PFAS adsorption, removal, or degradation experiments to assess equilibrium, plateau behavior, or reaction completion, and describe how this timing is reported to depend on the reaction speed and the specific system behavior.

Summarize what the reported kinetic sampling strategies reveal about the transition from early uptake to equilibrium or endpoint conditions in PFAS experiments, only where the underlying studies explicitly support such interpretations, and without implying that a single fixed set of time intervals is universally applicable.

claim_groups.canonical_proposition: PFAS adsorption kinetic experiments use dense early-time sampling (from minutes to a few hours) to capture rapid initial uptake, with specific time grids such as 30–480 minutes for PAC systems and early-hour windows (≤6 h) for other adsorbents.
claim_groups.central_proposition: In reported PFAS adsorption studies, kinetic sampling strategies include multiple early sampling points within the first minutes to hours to resolve the rapid initial uptake phase, such as Son et al.'s 30–480 min sampling on PAC and Militao et al.'s observation that >80% PFOS adsorption occurred within the first 6 h, as well as Chaudhary et al.'s systems where PFOS reached complete removal within 2 h and GenX reached equilibrium after 6 h.
material_qualifiers: powder-activated carbon (PAC) adsorption of nine PFASs from surface water (Son et al. 2020)
alginate-encapsulated rice-straw biochar beads adsorbing PFOS (Militao et al. 2023)
regenerable carbonaceous adsorbents removing PFOS and GenX in mixed PFAS/Cd(II) systems (Chaudhary et al. 2025)
claim_groups.full_rule: Give full credit if the answer notes that kinetic sampling strategies in the cited PFAS adsorption systems include multiple early-time sampling points designed to capture rapid initial uptake, explicitly mentioning at least one concrete time grid or time window (e.g., 30–480 min in Son et al., >80% PFOS uptake within the first 6 h in Militao et al., or PFOS complete removal within 2 h and GenX equilibrium at 6 h in Chaudhary et al.).
claim_groups.partial_rule: Give partial credit if the answer correctly notes that these studies report rapid initial adsorption within an early time window but does not clearly describe the corresponding sampling intervals or conflates early-time behavior with general equilibrium behavior.
claim_groups.contradiction_rule: Mark as contradictory if the answer claims that early-time sampling is sparse or unnecessary in these systems, or if it asserts that initial uptake is slow in any of the cited studies despite the evidence of fast early adsorption.

raw_result.reference_answer:
Across the PFAS adsorption studies represented in the supplied evidence, kinetic sampling strategies are structured to resolve both rapid early uptake and later-time approach to plateau or equilibrium, with specific time grids tuned to the system behavior rather than following a single universal schedule.

For adsorption of nine PFASs on powder-activated carbon (PAC) from surface water, Son et al. report that sorption kinetics were measured as removal efficiency versus time at 30, 60, 120, 240, 360, and 480 minutes at 10 mg/L PAC. They note that “the adsorption rate of all the PFASs was initially fast, indicating that ~70% of removal was accomplished within 30 min” and that for several PFASs “70–80% and 90% of the adsorption process was accomplished within 30 and 60 min, respectively.” This sampling grid, with multiple points in the first 1–2 hours, captures the rapid initial uptake phase. Later points out to 240–480 minutes are used to follow the system toward steady behavior: Son et al. state that “constant efficiency was observed at ~240 min” and that “the others required 360 min to reach 90% adsorption.” Thus, in this PAC system, kinetic sampling is dense enough at early times to quantify the fast initial removal and extended long enough to see the transition to a constant-efficiency regime and near-endpoint conditions, with different PFASs approaching 90% adsorption at different contact times.

In Militao et al.’s study of PFOS removal using alginate-encapsulated rice-straw biochar, the temporal pattern is resolved at the scale of hours. They report that “PFOS uptake was relatively fast with > 80 % of the adsorption achieved within the first 6 h followed by slow kinetics that plateaued within 16 h.” The description of an “initial fast adsorption stage” followed by “slow kinetics that plateaued” indicates that sampling covered the initial hours to capture rapid uptake and was extended to at least ~16 hours to observe the plateau. These data show a clear transition: most adsorption occurs in the early 6-hour window, while additional contact time mainly reveals a slowing approach to a plateau, which defines the endpoint for this system.

Chaudhary et al. examine PFAS (including PFOS and GenX) adsorption on regenerable carbonaceous adsorbents under mixed PFAS/Cd(II) conditions and likewise report distinct early and later kinetic regimes on the timescale of hours. They state that “PFOS displayed the fastest adsorption rate, reaching complete removal (10 mg g−1) within 2 h whereas GenX exhibited the slowest uptake reaching equilibrium after 6 h of reaction time.” Their discussion emphasizes that “the time required to reach the PFAS adsorption equilibrium is strongly dependent on the adsorbent properties.” To illustrate this dependence, they summarize literature where PFOS and PFOA adsorption on granular activated carbon (GAC) required 168 h for equilibrium, while powdered activated carbon (PAC) in another study gave equilibrium within 4 h for PFOS and PFOA; additional reports cited include equilibrium times of 24 h for PFOS, ~120 h for PFOA, and ~15 h for PFOA and PFOS on PAC. Together, these examples show that endpoint sampling in PFAS adsorption experiments can range from a few hours to several days, depending on adsorbent type and PFAS identity, and that kinetic experiments are typically continued until equilibrium or a clear plateau is reached for the specific system.

Taken as a whole, the evidence shows that PFAS kinetic experiments commonly employ early-time sampling that is fine-grained enough (minutes to a few hours) to capture rapid initial uptake phases, followed by extended sampling (hours to days) to characterize the transition to constant efficiency or plateaued adsorption. The transition from fast uptake to slower, plateau-like behavior is explicitly documented in multiple systems: ~70% removal in 30 minutes with constant efficiency at ~240 minutes on PAC; >80% PFOS removal within 6 hours and plateau by 16 hours on alginate-biochar; complete PFOS removal within 2 hours and GenX equilibrium at 6 hours on certain carbonaceous adsorbents; and equilibrium times from 4 to 168 hours in other GAC and PAC systems. These observations also demonstrate that both early uptake dynamics and endpoint timing depend strongly on adsorbent properties and PFAS-specific interactions, so the reported strategies illustrate principles for scheduling kinetic sampling but do not support a single fixed set of time intervals as universally applicable across all PFAS adsorption, removal, or degradation experiments.
